title: How do you handle very large IN clauses, for example filtering by 10,000 ids, in JPA without hurting performance or hitting database limits?
shortTitle: Large IN clauses: chunking and alternatives?
topicTitle: Performance: Large IN, Dirty Checking, OSIV
keyPoints: Databases limit and penalize huge IN lists: Oracle caps at 1,000 literals, PostgreSQL slows as the list grows.
Large IN clauses defeat prepared-statement plan caching because every list size generates a unique query string.
Chunking splits the ID list into bounded batches (500-1000 each), keeping each query within limits and cacheable.
Array-join passes IDs as a single database array and uses = ANY(:ids) for one efficient query on PostgreSQL.
Server-side filtering keeps IDs in the database as a subquery or join, avoiding round-trips entirely.
Hibernate's in_clause_parameter_padding pads IN lists to power-of-two sizes for better plan cache hit rates.
Prefer server-side filtering when IDs originate from the same database, array-join for external ID sets, and chunking for portability.

s1_definition.oneliner: Never dump 10,000 literals into one IN clause: chunk into bounded batches, pass as a database array and join, or keep the filter server-side as a subquery.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Chunking** -- splits the ID list into bounded partitions (e.g., 500-1000 each), runs one IN query per chunk, and combines results in the application.
- **Array-join** -- passes all IDs as a single database array (e.g., PostgreSQL `= ANY(:ids)` or `unnest(:ids)`) and joins in one query.
- **Server-side filter** -- expresses the ID filter as a subquery or join so the IDs never leave the database: `WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM flagged_accounts)`.
- **IN clause limit** -- Oracle caps at 1,000 literals per IN clause; PostgreSQL accepts more but degrades with parse time and plan cache bloat.
- **in_clause_parameter_padding** -- Hibernate setting that pads IN lists to the next power-of-two size so varying list lengths hit the same cached query plan.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the fraud team has a list of 10,000 suspicious account numbers to look up. Handing the clerk a single slip listing all 10,000 numbers is unwieldy: the clerk chokes, and some systems reject slips longer than 1,000 lines. Instead, you either hand over the numbers in neat bundles of 500 (chunking), write all 10,000 into a scratch register the clerk already has and say "match against this register" (array-join), or point the clerk to the flagged accounts already recorded in the system (server-side filter).

sections.s6_takeaway:
Dumping thousands of IDs into a single IN clause is a classic mistake in JPA applications. Oracle rejects lists longer than 1,000 entries, and PostgreSQL accepts them but generates an enormous query string that defeats prepared-statement plan caching and slows parsing. The fix depends on where the IDs come from.

When the IDs originate from the same database, a server-side subquery is the best approach: no IDs travel to the application and back, and the database planner optimizes the query internally. When the IDs come from an external source and you use PostgreSQL, passing them as a single array with = ANY(:ids) executes in one efficient query with no literal-count limit. For portability across databases, chunking splits the list into bounded batches of 500-1000 and combines results.

In our National Bank of India system, when the fraud team has 10,000 suspicious account IDs from an external file, the array-join approach handles them in a single efficient query. When those suspicious accounts are already recorded in a flagged_accounts table, a server-side subquery avoids moving IDs over the wire entirely. Hibernate's in_clause_parameter_padding setting pads variable-size IN lists to power-of-two sizes so the plan cache is not polluted by every unique list length.

Remember one sentence: prefer server-side subqueries when IDs originate in the database, use array-join for external ID sets on PostgreSQL, and fall back to bounded chunking for portability, never dumping thousands of literals into one IN clause.
